title: Make the query do less
summary: Write a filtered aggregate, read a plan, and connect long-lived snapshots to query performance.

scenario.briefing: The revenue report scans every order, includes cancelled and refunded rows, and ignores the year filter. It also runs inside one long transaction that holds a snapshot for an hour. Fix the query first, then read the plan and the snapshot cost.

objectives.description: Identify scan, function, and projection problems in a plan.
Connect long snapshots to bloat and vacuum.

hints: Filter status and the date range before grouping.
Join customers only for the name you return.
Aggregate paid revenue and order count per customer.
Order by revenue descending and keep five rows.

misconceptions.description: Counting cancelled and refunded orders as revenue.
misconceptions.testDescription: Excludes cancelled, refunded, and out-of-range orders.
misconceptions.feedback: Revenue needs paid orders in the reporting period. Counting every row inflates both the count and the total.

misconceptions.description: Selecting every column so no index can cover the query.
misconceptions.feedback: Select only the columns the report needs. A narrow projection can use a covering index and reduces transfer.

misconceptions.description: Believing a long read transaction has no cost.
misconceptions.feedback: Readers do not block writers under MVCC, but a long snapshot keeps old row versions alive and delays vacuum, growing bloat.

misconceptions.description: Adding an index for every column to fix a slow query.
misconceptions.feedback: Indexes cost writes and storage. Measure the plan and index the filters and ordering the query actually uses.

sections.title: Filter and aggregate close to the data
sections.body: A revenue query should discard cancelled, refunded, and out-of-period rows before grouping. The fewer rows that reach the sort and aggregate, the less work and memory the query needs.

sections.title: Read the plan, not the stopwatch
sections.body: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows actual rows, loops, time, and buffer reads. A sequential scan is not automatically wrong, but a function on an indexed column or a wide projection can prevent the index you expected.

sections.title: Snapshots have a maintenance cost
sections.body: PostgreSQL readers do not block writers, but a long repeatable-read transaction holds an old snapshot. Old row versions cannot be vacuumed, so bloat and index size grow. Keep reporting transactions short or use a replica.

Reading every row of a table because no index answers the query.
The consistent view of data a transaction uses for reads.
Space held by dead row versions that vacuum has not reclaimed.
An index that contains every column a query needs.

steps.title: Write the revenue report
steps.prompt: Edit revenue.sql. Return name, order_count, and revenue_cents for paid orders placed in 2025, grouped by customer, highest revenue first, limited to five rows.
hints: Filter status = 'paid' and the 2025 date range in the WHERE clause.
Join customers to orders to get the name.
Group by the customer and aggregate count plus total cents.
Order by the revenue alias descending and apply LIMIT 5.

files.content:
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(o.total_cents) AS revenue_cents
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC;

database.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE customers (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

tests.description: Excludes cancelled, refunded, and out-of-range orders.

steps.title: Read the plan
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Find the scan on the large table.
Look for a function wrapped around an indexed column.
Check whether the query returns columns it does not use.
Revise the query: reduce the projection and remove the function from the filter.

artifact.title: EXPLAIN output
artifact.caption: The customer lookup joins orders and filters on lower(email).
artifact.content:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18420.00 rows=12 width=212) (actual time=0.031..182.440 rows=12 loops=1)
  Filter: (lower((customer_email)::text) = 'ada@example.edu'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 499988
  Buffers: shared hit=14200 read=4220
Planning Time: 0.210 ms
Execution Time: 182.810 ms

Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE lower(customer_email) = 'ada@example.edu';

findings.label: The query scans the whole orders table.
Wrapping customer_email in lower() prevents a plain index on the column from being used.
SELECT * forces a wide projection that cannot be covered by a narrow index.
Adding LIMIT without ORDER BY does not make the result deterministic.
Adding an index always improves a query.

verdicts.label: Revise the filter and projection, then measure again

steps.explanation: The function on the column and the wide projection defeat useful indexes. Fix the query shape first, then add a matching index if the plan needs one.

steps.title: What does a long snapshot cost?
steps.prompt: A report holds a repeatable-read transaction open for an hour while writers continue. What is the main cost?
hints: PostgreSQL uses multi-version concurrency control.
Readers do not block writers in MVCC.
Old row versions must remain visible to the snapshot.
Vacuum cannot reclaim those versions, so bloat grows.

options.label: Old row versions stay visible to the snapshot, so vacuum cannot reclaim them and bloat grows
Writers are blocked for the whole hour
There is no cost because reads never affect writes

quiz.explanation: MVCC lets readers and writers proceed, but a long snapshot keeps dead versions alive. Keep reporting transactions short or run them on a replica.

steps.title: Measure, then change one thing
hints: Plans and buffers are evidence; stopwatches are noisy.
Indexes have write and storage costs.
Pagination needs a stable order.
Select measurement, narrow projections, matching indexes, and keyset pagination; reject indexing every column.

statements.label: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows actual rows, time, and buffer use.
Selecting only the needed columns can enable a covering index.
Every index adds write and storage cost, so add only those a query shape needs.
Keyset pagination avoids the growing offset cost of OFFSET pagination.
Indexing every column is the safest way to speed up reads.

steps.explanation: Query performance comes from measuring the plan, narrowing the data, and adding the smallest index that serves the access pattern.
